speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxlon (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: KURT MEYER-JOHANN NEITZ STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO REVIEW OF SENTENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the interest which has been expressed by a number of members from time to time in the Kurt Meyer case, I should like to make a brief statement with respect to his case and that of Johann Neitz, the only two German war criminals convicted by Canadian military courts still serving sentences. Their sentences are being served in a British administration prison at Werl, Germany.
The terms of the agreements between the occupying powers and Germany provided for the review of the sentences of war criminals. In view of the delay in bringing these agreements into effect, some time ago boards were set up in each of the British, United States and French zones to review the sentences of all convicted German war criminals still held in custody in those zones.
The Canadian government appointed Brigadier Sherwood Lett, Q.C., C.B.E., D.S.O., M.C., E.D., of Vancouver, to represent it as an observer when the cases of Meyer and Neitz were considered by the board set up in the British zone. This board has reviewed the sentences now being served by Kurt Meyer and Johann Neitz and has recommended that in both cases the sentences be commuted to fourteen years.
The recommendation of the board in each case was unanimous and Brigadier Lett has recommended that the government should accept the recommendation of the board.
After the most careful consideration of the circumstances the government has accepted the recommendation of the board.
Both Meyer and Neitz will be eligible for such remission of their sentences as they may have earned or may earn in accordance with the rules in force in the prison where they are confined and which are laid down by the British custodian.
I might add that I understand the reviewing boards' recommendations in each zone have
been accepted in each case by the governments of France, the United Kingdom and the United States.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, January 14, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Cote-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair:
That it is expedient to amend the Post Office Act to increase the rates of postage on letters posted in Canada from the 1st day of April, 1954,
(a)	on each letter for delivery within the postal area in which it is posted, from three cents to four cents for the first ounce or fraction of an ounce, and from one cent to two cents for each additional ounce or fraction of an ounce, and
(b)	on each letter posted within one postal area for delivery in another postal area from four cents to five cents for the first ounce or fraction of an ounce, and from two cents to three cents for each additional ounce or fraction of an ounce.

As I have indicated, the estimated effect of the proposed increase on the revenues of the department will be approximately $15 million. If you look at the Postmaster General's report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1953, page 3, you will find statistics which will enable you to check this estimate. I am now trying to answer directly the question: How did you arrive at this estimate? There are approximately 1,500 million pieces of first-class mail which, at one cent an item, will give you $15 million. To this should be added additional postage on the items which require more than the initial rate of postage. The total increase we estimate will be in the neighbourhood of $15,750,000. Against this, we must deduct the items forwarded by air mail, on which at present an air mail surcharge is paid. We estimate that this will be in the neighbourhood of $900,000, so that you will see that the amount we expect to obtain is slightly less than $15 million.
Reference has been made to the rates of postage paid in the United States. In this connection I would suggest that you examine the financial statement of the United States Post Office Department and look also at the deficit. I could further support the case for the increase by referring to the rates paid in other postal administrations, but I prefer to deal with this matter in relation to the Canadian economy.
Reference was also made and opposition expressed on the one hand to so-called hidden subsidies, but on the other hand it was suggested that the additional costs to which I have referred should be overcome by charging them to the general surplus. In the same breath some have criticized the subsidies and they have suggested them. These two approaches appear to me to be inconsistent. As far as I am concerned, I prefer to make an outright statement as to what the cost will be and, as I have already indicated, have those persons who use the service meet the additional expenditure. This seems to me to be the most equitable and straightforward way.
Some hon. members have referred to the surplus which the Postmaster General's reports show over the past twenty years. I would ask these gentlemen to bear in mind that during these years the department's revenues were augmented by the amount of postage stamps which were being used in payment of the tax on cheques or other
[Mr. Cote.l
remittances. Had this not been the case, then the surpluses to which they refer would have been materially reduced, if not dissipated entirely.
This year no postage stamps have been used in payment of the tax on cheques. As a result the surplus of $6,500,000 shown in the accounts for the last fiscal year will, it is estimated, become a deficit of at least $1 million.
It has been suggested that the department should not anticipate the increased expenditures, but should wait until the deficit actually occurs. I might say it is not a question of anticipation but one of fact. The increased rates of payment to postal employees are effective from December 1, 1953. Adjusted higher rates have already been paid to rural mail couriers, and adjustments are continually taking place. Arrangements are already being made for the recruiting of the additional staffs required to give the five-day forty-hour week service, and there is already a potential deficit as the revenues have barely been maintained compared to last year, whereas the total expenditure has increased during the nine-month period already elapsed by $4 million.
I appreciate the reference made to that great Liberal, Sir William Mulock, and to the fact that, while he was postmaster general, he reduced the letter rate of postage from 3 cents to 2 cents. At that time the opposition opposed the decrease. Now they oppose the increase. But the point I wish to make is that in 1898 the initial salary of postal employees was $400 a year. Now it is $2,400 a year, an increase of 500 per cent. The letter rate now proposed, namely five cents, would mean an increase of 150 per cent over the rates charged more than 50 years ago.
I now come to two specific cases. The hon. member for Vancouver East made the statement that direct air mails from Vancouver to Calgary were carried on the Canadian Pacific Air Lines rather than on the direct Trans-Canada Air Lines. Such is not the case.
He also made reference to mails being carried on the Canadian Pacific Railway to Kamloops and then transferred to the Canadian National Railways. There is nothing wrong with this. It is good post office practice and is simply the most economical utilization of space paid for and available.
I believe he also stated that he had been informed that the department was endeavouring to eliminate the night differential granted to postal employees. We have no

such thought in mind. I am afraid that he is getting his information from an unreliable source.
Another point which was raised related to an incident mentioned by his leader which happened a number of years ago where mails were stated to have been carried in what seemed to be an illogical manner. The department does not claim to be perfect. Errors are bound to occur in an organization of this size, but there is usually some justifiable reason for the action taken. We are always desirous of being told when our decisions do not seem to be logical or justifiable, and we shall always be glad to explain the situation, if necessary to make inquiries, and, if any reasonable improvement can be made with due regard to economical operation, it will be done.
Now that we are talking about the service, let me give you some indication of the additional service which has been given by the Post Office Department during the past ten years. This is in answer to some suggestions that the service was poor or even worse. The number of cities where door to door delivery is given has increased from 89 to 127, or 38 additional cities. The number of additional homes served by letter carrier during this period is over 750,000. In the rural areas the number of patrons receiving rural mail delivery has increased from 290.000 to 410,000, an increase of 120,000 boxes. Therefore in the urban and rural areas over 870,000 additional families have been given individual service to their own homes or boxes in the last ten years.
In the outlying districts postal service has assisted in the development of such areas as Yellowknife, at points where there are uranium and other mining projects and where there are water power and aluminum developments such as at Kitimat in British Columbia. Additional service has also been given to Sept lies in the province of Quebec in connection with the iron developments in Ungava, Labrador and northern Quebec. Many other such cases could be enumerated. As a matter of fact, the amount which we are paying for air stage services, that is, services to outlying and pioneer points, is approximately $1,500,000 a year.
May I come now to my hon. friend, the hon. member for Eglinton. He exhibited to the house several envelopes to indicate the standard of service. I know he did not knowingly wish to be unfair, and he was good enough to give me the exhibits so that due inquiry could be made. This has been done. The minister has dealt rather generally with the situation, Mr. Chairman, and to his own satisfaction has partly disposed of the example given by the hon. member for Eglinton concerning certain delays. I doubt, however, if there is any hon. member in this house who is not well aware of the delays that have occurred. Many have been ready to recognize the difficulties with which the post office department is confronted, but to suggest that there have not been extensive delays wholly unrelated to misaddressing, or lack of address, is simply to deny the facts that are in the minds of almost all hon. members here.
There have been comments, and not unfriendly comments, about the change in the postal service in this country. For instance, there was the statement made in more than one city that mail posted in Britain was being delivered here more quickly than mail posted and delivered in the same city. Having said that I think that every hon. member here knows from his own experience or her own experience that we have no more loyal, trustworthy and devoted civil servants in Canada than those who are delivering and handling the mail in this country. There is probably no public servant who is so closely in touch with the daily life of every one of us as the postman who delivers the mail at our door. He is practically a friend of the family. He is very much a part of the life of each family.
I am satisfied that there is nothing but praise and commendation for the way in which those who are carrying out the daily routine of the mail service have been performing their functions. The criticism which has been directed to the situation which exists is a criticism directed to the administration of the department. It is a criticism such as was made by the business firm which

Post Office Act
inquired into the activities of that department less than a year ago. It is a criticism of the kind that was placed, as a matter of record, by the firm of J. D. Woods and Gordon, and referred to in this house, although not in detail. It is criticism of the failure of the department to implement recommendations that could have been carried into effect.
The minister is quite correct when he says that it is so easy to suggest that increases of any kind should not be made, because no one of us likes paying more than we paid before for any other service. This, however, is something a little different from those ordinary increases which take place in regard to the daily necessities of our life. The minister has said, and it is no way an unfair suggestion, that we should look at the comparison between the increase in postage rates and the increase in the costs of other public services of a similar nature. At first glance that seems a cogent argument. There is another argument, however. The rise in cost of service has been general throughout the world. We must not only look at the increase in rates in relation to the increase in the cost of other services. It would be advisable for us to look at our rates in comparison with rates for similar services in other countries where there are similar social and economic conditions.
With that thought in mind, naturally we first direct our attention to the United States. We find that at a time when we are asked to approve an increase to five cents for the first ounce, in the United States, where in the ordinary course of events the cost of service is certainly not less than in Canada, they pay two cents for first-class mail placed in post offices where there is not a pick-up postal service, and three cents for the first ounce where there is the ordinary pick-up service.
In Britain they start with a higher weight. In Britain the unit of weight is the first two ounces. There they charge just over three cents, which is the present value of the two-pence-halfpenny postage. If we examine the rate that is charged for that service in countries of similar economic and social structure, I think we shall find that we have the highest rate in the world for that ordinary service to the homes of our people where family messages and the other communications are carried in this way.
The attitude on this occasion is simply one of showing where the department estimates that new costs are going to be incurred but there is no suggestion of what the department could do or has done to bring about some of those economies that might be effected. Already the minister has expressed
[Mr. Drew.l
his approval when one hon. member last night referred to a great postmaster general, and I might say he is regarded as a great postmaster general by all Canadians, namely the late Sir William Mulock. Sir William Mulock became famous not only in Canada but throughout the world because of the reduction of postage rates to what was then known as the penny postage, the two-cent stamp. He was reversing a trend that had gone on for some time. He was carrying forward a trend that had developed from 1851. To show the changes that had taken place, in 1851 the lowest charge for a letter was 18 cents, and then we came to the point in 1898 when living expenses were certainly far higher, and when any comparison of the cost of ordinary services would suggest on the present basis an increase. Nevertheless we find that there was actually a decrease at that time. No matter what some people may have thought at the time, I believe that because of the general acceptance, over the years, of the soundness of the position taken by Sir William Mulock at that time, it might be well to refer not only to the words which have been quoted but to certain other views that he expressed.
At column 5525 of Hansard of 1898 I find these words:
I venture to say that these statistics establish beyond all question that the reduction in the letter rate promotes an increase in the number of letters, in the volume of business and in the revenue, and at any rate it is essential to the interests of the country that there should be the cheapest possible mail communication.
May I say that this statement has found general acceptance throughout the years: -that there should be the cheapest possible mail communication.

The fact that we shall have a five-cent stamp to perform the same service as a three-cent stamp will perform in the United States, just across that long border, is something that is not to be completely disregarded. After all, there are large business enterprises at many points along that border in cities from the Atlantic to the Pacific, some of them larger than others, some of them enormous businesses, sending out many thousands of pieces of mail every day. There would be nothing illegal in anybody getting in an automobile and driving across the boundary and posting these several thousand pieces of mail for three cents apiece and sending them into Canada at the reduced rate, below what they would pay if they posted the mail in Canada in the first place for delivery within our own country. I do not say that that is an impossibility. It would be a perfectly reasonable thing to do when in many cases they are just as close to a post office in the United States as they would be to a post office in a Canadian city.
Naturally Canadians want to support their own services and naturally there would be criticism if Canadians went outside the country to do that. However, we found in the case of cigarettes and a number of other things that people do look at the dollars and even at the cents. We are talking about cents in this case but those cents can accumulate to a great amount. No better evidence of the fact that many a mickle makes a muckle is to be found than in the amount of revenue the Postmaster General expects to obtain by this increase of one cent. Surely that is a fine example to our children of the law of economics and how much a cent may mean if there are enough of them put together.

more prosperous days ahead, that it would be wise for us Canadians to remember that we live in a competitive world where price along with quality is going to determine whether the things that we produce are going to be sold.
This is not the first time that I have raised this point in the house, nor is it the first time that it has been raised by other members of the Conservative party. We have sought to emphasize that in a period of increasing world competition taxes of all kinds and burdens of every nature which increase the ultimate cost of the thing we sell must be examined, not only from the point of view of the burden on the individual but from the point of view of the effect it will have upon a nation which is today more dependent than any other nation in the world upon the maintenance of its export business for the continuance of its prosperity.
I suggest that this is not the time to be increasing the tax burden, and this is a tax for a service. This is not a time to be increasing this burden when we should be looking for every opportunity to save even one cent. We must recognize that this becomes a part of the general cost of doing business and selling the things that we produce.
There is another feature that arises in the cost of postage. Unless the newspapers of Canada from one side of the country to the other have been quite wrong in their comments about delays in deliveries, there has been an increasing number of delays in the delivery of our mail. Even if it is a question only of three days instead of one, that is important. One clear demonstration of the efficiency of organized society is the speed with which people can communicate with each other within that society.
In other countries they have been increasing the speed of delivery. In other countries, even where the costs are high, there are several deliveries a day. In some of the larger cities in other countries a letter posted one day is delivered the same day. We should be striving to improve the effective delivery and more frequent delivery of our mail, instead of having a less frequent delivery with unexplainable delays of one, two and three days in the delivery of business mail.
All this tends to persuade people to use other services such as the telegraph and the telephone. Who knows but that may be one of the reasons why so many millions of dollars have been added to the cost of telegrams sent by this government. It may be due to the fact that the government departments know that their own Post Office Department is so slow that, if they want to get

Post Office Act
a quick answer they had better use the telegraph or the telephone. We have been curious as to the tremendous increase in the cost of telegrams and telephone calls and perhaps that is the explanation. It would be interesting if we could get that answer. Certainly a higher cost of postal service will encourage people to use these other services.
We pride ourselves on the efficiency of our telegraph and telephone services. I think we can say with satisfaction that they are not surpassed in any country of the world, even when we consider the long distances of this country. The Post Office Department should be doing everything they can to provide a cheap service by mail which offers a means of communication to the masses of our people. The rate should be such as to encourage them to use it more and more.
The attitude of the government in regard to these costs is demonstrated by the fact that emphasis has been placed upon a supposed loss of $7,500,000 because of the elimination of the stamp tax. Are we to believe from that statement that the Post Office Department can sell $7,500,000 worth of stamps without additional cost? Does it cost nothing to produce stamps? Whether they are right or wrong, some newspapers in this country have suggested that some stamps look as though they had been produced without much cost.

The government knew perfectly well when it removed the stamp tax that this result was going to follow. It pointed out how convenient it was going to be not to have to put stamps on cheques; but it is only now that we are being told that the taxpayers of Canada have got to pay for it in another way. When today the minister tells us that some of these expenses could not be anticipated, may I remind him that the general policy of a five-day 40-hour week was being instituted some considerable time ago, and that this must surely have been in the minds of officials of the department at that time.
No, Mr. Chairman; this is another case where the pleasant thing was done before the election. And now, with all the smiling blandness of the explanation given by the minister here today and yesterday, we are asked to approve the adding of this burden to the postal service of Canada.
I was interested in the statement made yesterday by one hon. member when he said that if big businessmen were paying it this government would not be making the change. I do not quite understand that statement; but let us remember that, very largely, it was the big businessmen who paid the stamp tax, in so far as those big businessmen may be regarded as paying what the corporations pay. But we know perfectly well that the costs of those things are added to the cost of doing business in this country anyway; and they are deductible for income tax purposes. This was known very well by the minister who is sponsoring the bill as well as by the minister who announced this increase in the price of postage stamps.
A good deal has been said about the cost of post offices across the country. The suggestion seems to be that we should not worry about an increase of this kind when we think about all that is being spent on post offices. Let me point out that post offices do not serve only in the handling of letters on which this postage will be paid. Those post offices handle registrations and special delivery services. Then, in addition to that, in most places the post office building houses the customs offices. In other places we find in the post office buildings the offices of the government annuities service as well as services rendered by the Department of Labour.
In short, post office buildings across this country are for the general service of the community. Certainly nothing I am saying suggests that we should be reckless in the handling of our postal service, or in any other services, or that we should disregard the costs. But having regard to the fact that our neighbours in the United States, who live lives very similar to ours and who are faced with costs very much like those we face, are called upon to pay only two or

three cents tor first-class postal service of this kind, I suggest it is very unsound, in this very competitive world, to ask our people to pay five cents for a similar service.
I repeat that we are not just dealing with one cent, or even with a five-cent piece which, on occasion, has been embarrassing to governments before. We are dealing with the total amount of this increase in a service that is closely associated with the daily lives of our people, perhaps more closely than any other service they receive from the government each day.
I suggest therefore that much more than a casual explanation of expected added costs should be given to us by the Postmaster General, who heads a department which has accumulated such enormous surpluses in years gone by. I know that reference has been made to them; but, having regard to the explanation offered today, may I remind the minister how easy it would have been to wait and see just exactly what the net result of changes being made would be, and whether certain things could not be done to expand the services offered by the Post Office Department through the introduction of new devices, such as have been introduced in the past to encourage the use of the postal service.
We know that over a period of 10 years the surpluses of this department amounted to $70,193,330.54, and that for the preceding 10 years the surpluses were $22,969,606.69, making a total of more than $93 million surplus in the last 20 years in the operations of this department, and at the lower stamp rates which have been in effect during that length of time.

speechtext: With all deference to you, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that this is an important part of this whole discussion because the reason given for the increase in rates is loss of revenue. I want to point out here why I believe that the loss of revenue which will take place because of the decrease in the air mail rate from seven cents to five cents is unjustified. I believe that, quite the reverse of regular mail, air mail is something for which a person can pay an extra fee if it is so important for him or her to have such mail delivered in a hurry. If I have to have a letter delivered somewhere in Canada faster than ordinary mail delivery will take it there, then I am perfectly willing to pay two or three cents extra to have that service. I am sure every Canadian feels exactly the same way about it. This is not regular postal delivery. I am going to make two suggestions to enable the Postmaster General to keep his service on a pay-as-you-go basis without increasing the general postal rate. The first is to leave the air mail rate at seven cents. According to simple arithmetic, a reduction of two cents on 32 million pieces of mail amounts to $640,000 a year, and leaving the air mail rate at seven cents would mean a saving of that amount. Then I come to my second suggestion. In his budget last year, the Minister of Finance cancelled the stamp tax on cheques. That matter has already been discussed by several members. The Minister of Finance estimated that it would cost the government $12 million to effect the cancellation of the stamp tax on cheques. That tax was borne largely by business, and very little by the ordinary people of the country.
The ordinary workingman receives his pay cheque, takes it to the bank and cashes it. When such cheque had a stamp affixed to it, the stamp was put there by the firm employing him. He cashes the cheque, takes the money home, gives most of it to his wife, keeps some for himself, and carries on for the next week or two. If the ordinary person has a bank account, it is usually a savings account and he issues relatively few cheques. To me the cancelling of the stamp tax on

Post Office Act
cheques was simply a pre-election inducement, shall we call it, to business. I do not know any ordinary citizens who were very elated about its cancellation, or felt that they benefited very much from it. It is something which everybody certainly accepts, but if it is a question of a choice between requiring people to affix a stamp on a cheque, and raising the general postal rate one cent right across the board, then to me there is no comparison.
The arithmetic of this whole thing adds up in this way. Last year the Post Office Department showed an operating surplus of $6 million. If the stamp tax on cheques had not been cancelled, that $6 million surplus, together with the $12 million which the Minister of Fiftance estimated it would cost the government to eliminate the stamp tax on cheques, would add up to $18 million. The Postmaster General estimates that his new expenses are going to run around $14 million. Therefore, according to my arithmetic, the Postmaster General and the government, if they would follow the suggestion I am making, would be able to show a surplus of $4 million, and it would not be necessary to tamper in any way with the general postal rates which affect the ordinary people of this country; the people whom we must protect. They are the people who are going to be hurt very materially by this general increase in postal rates. If the Postmaster General and the government feel that the Post Office Department must pay its own way, this is a suggestion how to do it. It is a suggestion which I feel will meet with the general approval of people throughout the country, and for that reason I recommend it most seriously to the Postmaster General for his consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take part in this discussion for a moment not so much as a politician or parliamentarian but as a philatelist, a stamp collector. I have one or two observations leading up to one point I have to offer. I am a member of the Saint John stamp club and, I think, still a member of the Canadian philatelic society. Stamp collectors generally have a pretty good idea of the whole picture so far as the stamp business is concerned.
First of all I should like to make an observation about our Canadian stamps. Back in the 1920's we turned out some very lovely, finely engraved and beautiful stamps which received attention all over the world. I refer particularly to the 50-cent Bluenose stamp which I think won an international prize at that time. But since the twenties our stamps have deteriorated greatly in their engraving,

and while Canadian stamps are generally very highly regarded by collectors in the sense that they are scarce and in demand on the market I do think we should note that our stamps have fallen off slightly in their beauty. When this increase goes through and new stamps are needed I think it might be noted that perhaps we could concentrate a little bit more on the standards that we followed formerly.
Another point, and one that is perhaps more important here, concerns the relative value of ordinary postage in other countries of the world. As a collector thumbs through his stamps he naturally notices the value of the stamps of these other countries that are found in the largest quantity, and I should like to take a minute now to compare the rates or values of stamps in the countries of Europe and elsewhere in the world. It was not possible for me to get any exact figures on the relative rates in other countries. I checked with the Post Office Department, but they did not have any information. I quite appreciate that a request for such information would be unusual, and also difficult to fill. The rates would have to be translated into our own currency, and in addition to that some of the countries are on the metric system of weights.
Nevertheless, from a quick observation, from talking with people who have travelled and from my own travels, I have gathered some figures which I should like to throw into this discussion. I believe that in Poland it costs six cents to send a postcard. Czechoslovakia and Bulgaria are both a cent less than that figure. The other figures decrease generally until you reach countries with a better culture and a better standard of living. I happen to know that in Portugal, Egypt and India the rates for both postcards and ordinary mail are very high.
Turning to Great Britain and the United States, the two countries which are perhaps most comparable with our own today in terms of general enlightenment and culture, I believe that the postal rate in England is one and a half pence. I am still sure that the postal rate in the United States is three cents, although the Postmaster General hinted there might be an increase. I know that in his state of the union address, President Eisenhower recommended moving the rate to four cents, but no action has been taken in congress. We have rates, therefore, in both England and the United States of about three cents.
Now, the conclusions I shall draw from these one or two observations, as a stamp collector, are alarming. When other people who are familiar with the situation see that

countries with depressed conditions, that do not have the fine standard of living we have, charge high rates for this necessary service and the other countries with better living conditions have a lower postal rate, and this proposed increase in Canada will be going in the direction of the depressed countries, then people will be forced to conclude that Canada is stepping down to the levels of those countries. I know that my stamp collecting friends will agree with that.

I should like to comment briefly on this proposed increase in the postal rate, mainly because yesterday the hon. member for Charlotte made an observation to the effect that people in the various parts of Canada were not too interested in the effects of the proposal. I have received several communications on the subject, and as the information arising from this discussion is scattered across the country through the medium of the press, I am sure I shall receive further communications. I believe that is to be expected because, as was pointed out by various speakers, the people of Canada, like the people of all democratic countries, have come to regard the provision of a reasonably inexpensive postal service as a part of their democratic heritage.
It seems that it is an unwritten principle that they identify the provision of cheap postal service with the provision of highways, bridges and other means of communication. The proposed increase, therefore, even though it seems to be infinitesimally small, as it is in this case, will draw considerable protest from the people of Canada.
I should like to make one brief suggestion to the Postmaster General on this matter. During the debate several members have made statements praising the efficiency of the employees in the Post Office Department. I am rather inclined to conclude that, as a result of the improvement in working conditions recently made, the introduction of the five-day, forty-hour week and the increase in wages, you are going to see a further increase in efficiency. It might be that the increased volume of work handled by the employees would tend to offset the increased expenditures that have resulted from these improvements. I say this because from a very narrow knowledge of the subject-I have knowledge only of the conditions in our local post office in Brandon-I would be inclined to think that if efficiency is the same in every post office as it is in Brandon we might increase revenue to such an extent by the improvement in productivity that it would more than offset the expected $12 million deficit.
For example, some statistics I have in front of me relating to the Brandon post office
Post Office Act
show that in 1925, with an annual revenue of $110,600, there were 44 employees. In 1952 with a revenue of $217,120, there were 41 employees, a decrease of three employees and almost a doubling of the revenues. In terms of the employee situation, before the changeover to one delivery per day there were 15 walks in the city of Brandon. As a result of the decreased frequency of service the number of walks was decreased to 12 and eventually cut to 11. Since the improvement in the salary situation, and notwithstanding the rapid expansion of the city of Brandon since the war, the number of walks stands at eleven and a half.
I was rather curious about the half a walk, so I inquired about it. I understand that as a result of appeals from the local office it was decided to put on a carrier for four hours a day, and this constitutes half a walk. It seems to me here is efficiency par excellence. In our local post office unit with revenues going up and work increasing-no doubt the figures for 1953 will be considerably above those I quoted for 1952-there has been a decrease in the personnel employed. I see no reason why, if such efficiency is possible right across Canada, sufficient savings might not be made to meet the expected deficit.
In any case the proposal is of such a controversial nature that it would be wise to postpone a decision for two or three years to ascertain the effect of the new situation in the Post Office Department. If, as the member for Charlotte concluded yesterday, there is no undue anxiety in the minds of the people of Canada concerning this one-cent postal increase, it would not do any harm to the government if it waited even until a preelection year before introducing this measure.

speechtext:
I rise to support hon. members who have spoken against the introduction of this resolution at this time. Some members of this group rose yesterday and asked for a vote on the matter. It is a pleasure to listen to the explanations of the genial and courteous Postmaster General. He has always been nonchalant in his answers, and courteous throughout the whole debate. I think he is taking the matter more seriously now than when he first introduced the resolution. The preponderance of evidence which hon. members have brought forward in this debate indicates that at this time the people of Canada do not like this increase in the postal rate in any way, shape or form, and are not in agreement with it.
In his explanation this afternoon the minister told us there are only two methods by which we can meet the situation which faces the post office at the present time. He said that owing to the introduction of the five-day

Post Office Act
and forty-hour week there have been increases in costs. I want to suggest to him that the two methods which he indicated, namely an increase in the cost of postal service or subsidization of the Post Office Department, are not the only ways by which improvements can be brought about. Economies in the operation of the post office could be effected. If his department would seriously undertake economies I am sure that improvements could be brought about.
I suggest to the minister that the United States post office department has just done that very thing in one operation. They investigated different methods by which they could inaugurate economies, and they found that by using nylon mail bags instead of the heavier canvas bags they could save the post office department $800,000. That change is to be instituted in the near future. I know very well that the United States post office department handles a great deal more mail than we do in Canada, but I want to promote the idea of that change here in Canada, and I am sure we could make a proportionate saving in this country.
It surprises me that 125 days after the August 10 election we should have this government introducing a resolution such as this. Prior to the election they brought in a so-called election budget, which was given a great deal of publicity in Canada. I know that in my own province the Liberal candidates referred to it quite often. Frequent reference was made to the discontinuance of the 3-cent tax on cheques.
It seems to me this government has some sort of tax malady. In my school days we used to hear of trigger-happy people who would go out and shoot up everybody. Now we have a government that is tax-happy. Before the election they became affected in some way, and they found ways and means of reducing the revenue of the government by eliminating the tax on cheques, and taking off a tax here and there. The Liberal candidates in the west went around the provinces indicating that the government was going to slash taxes, and suggested that if they were returned to power that sort of thing would continue. What do we find? Immediately after the government returns to Ottawa they ask hon. members to impose a tax on the mails of this country.
Let us look at this question. Yesterday the hon. member for Charlotte said he felt the people were willing to pay this extra amount. He said it would be big business who would pay the bulk of the increase. Today we are living in a complex society. It is quite different from 30 or 40 years ago. Today

many of our young people are in the armed forces and are away from home. This is going to be an important restriction on the people in the low-income brackets. The people we are concerned about are not the people in big business. They can take care of themselves. If we have a 7-cent air mail stamp they are able to put the 7-cent stamp on their mail and have it go by air. I am concerned with the people in the low-income brackets.
We have a government across the way who by their decontrol policy and tax policy are leaving with the people in the small income brackets only a small amount of money to take care of their needs. They have to budget very carefully. If we accept the truth of the statement that today our dollar is worth perhaps 50 cents, then it becomes obvious that every cent we take from the purchasing power of the people in low-income brackets will have an important effect on the livelihood of these people.
I feel quite confident, and I say it to the minister, that the young people in the armed services want to continue to correspond with their people at home. They want to continue writing to their people, and they are not worrying too much about fast mail service. If the minister cannot assure the committee that first-class mail will go by aeroplane, then I am sure these people would rather have the lower rate than the higher rate suggested.
I do not want to prolong this debate, but in view of what has happened the Postmaster General might tell the committee now, since he is bringing in this measure 125 days after the election, whether when election time rolls around three years from now we shall again have the 4-cent postage.

The minister referred to a commission or committee which over a period had investigated the Post Office Department with a view to improving its efficiency, or at least its effectiveness. Certainly my experience with the department has been such that I can make no criticism, but naturally when an experienced group of chartered accountants make what the minister has referred to as a full and complete examination there is no doubt that in their report generalized considerations and decisions would be arrived at.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, December 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Argue for the second reading of Bill No. 3, to amend the Canada Grain Act (distribution of box cars).

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am particularly pleased to rise at this time to speak in support of Bill No. 3, an act to provide for the distribution of box cars at a marketing point in accordance with the wishes of the farmers. I do so at this time because I had the opportunity, during the Christmas recess, to return to my constituency and discuss this proposal with the farmers in the various districts concerned, and I found that they were unanimously in favour of a system whereby they would have some say in the allocation of box cars among the elevators at a particular marketing point. They favour a principle whereby they would state their intentions of delivery to the various elevator companies, and the railways would then be obligated to deliver railway cars in response to their wishes.
In addressing the house the last time we were debating this motion, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) made the point that the car order book as at present constituted is perfectly adequate as a mechanism to allow the farmers to deliver grain to the elevators of their choice. He implied that there was no necessity for any further regulations in order to give the farmers the privilege of delivering to the elevators of their choice. In that regard I might state that the president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, Mr. J. H. Wesson, speaking to the annual convention of the pool, had this to say:
I notified the minister that as far as the pools were concerned our main interest was not to eliminate the car order book section but to do something by an amendment to the act to deal with the distribution of cars when the car order book section could not function under these conditions,
Canada Grain Act
-to deal with the distribution, not by regulation of the board of grain commissioners but by a definite amendment to the act.
The bill we have under debate is a definite amendment to the act that is aimed at distributing box cars according to the farmers' wishes. At the same time the memorandum to the government of Canada from the interprovincial farm union council in November of last year had this to say:
We realize that the present car order book provisions are inadequate to meet present conditions, and we submit they were not framed for such a purpose. We desire now, as we did when we appeared before the agricultural committee of the House of Commons last spring, to make a specific recommendation that the proposals put forward in the committee's report to the house on that occasion, following our presentation, be proceeded with immediately to review and revise the Canada Grain Act, including the section dealing with the car order book, and add a new section providing the farmer opportunity to deliver his grain to the elevator of his choice. However, we urge the retention of the present provision for the farmer to order a car in his proper turn to the loading platform or other place of his own choosing.
Our bill meets with the exact requirements as set out by the memorandum to the government from the interprovincial farm union council. I believe the two statements I have referred to would refute in its entirety the statement made by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) who, as reported at page 934 of Hansard, said:
... no demand has been made for it by the western farmers themselves.
As reported at page 936 of Hansard, the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that Mr. R. H. Milliken, solicitor for the Saskatchewan wheat pool and a lawyer, finds the legal terminology of our bill not to his liking. We do not profess to be lawyers. If Mr. Milliken takes exception to the legal terminology of our bill-and I maintain that is what he took exception to, and not the principle contained in it-then I suggest that the government themselves could improve on the legal wording by giving the task to one of the abundance of trained legal backbenchers so they would have something to do this session.
As practical farmers we all realize that delivery to the elevator that has the room is a most unsatisfactory criterion. On occasion I have been forced to deliver one load to each of three elevators because they filled up in that order. I have my own desires as to where I want to market my grain, and I do not want to be governed by the principle that there is room for only a certain amount of my grain in a certain elevator because the railways have allocated box cars in that particular proportion.

Canada Grain Act
This matter was taken up by a group of individuals in my constituency, and I have some highly interesting correspondence to prove the necessity for the inclusion in the Canada Grain Act of a principle whereby the railways would have definite guidance in the allocation of box cars at a marketing point in accordance with the wishes of the farmers. Here is a copy of a telegram sent to Superintendent E. Cutts of the Canadian National Railways at Saskatoon, copies of which were later sent to Mr. Mclvor and to Mr. Milner. The telegram reads as follows:
We the shipping committee as representatives of the wheat pool members of Springwater district do not see why Federal Grain with two licenses but only one agent, should get two-thirds of grain cars at this point when they continually show space, while the pool is plugged and patrons cannot deliver their quota to the elevator of their choice. It would seem to us that this being a democratic country there should be no reason why we cannot have sufficient cars to handle our quotas through our own pool elevator system.
That telegram was sent over the names of Mr. H. W. Turner, chairman, and Mr. R. C. Staples, secretary of the local wheat pool committee. They received in reply a telegram from Mr. Cutts. It was addressed to Mr. H. W. Turner, chairman, and Mr. Robert C. Staples, secretary, wheat pool committee, Springwater, Saskatchewan, and reads as follows:
Wheat board instructions require empties be supplied each elevator equally when they have grain to ship.
That is the answer they received from the railways. Here is the answer they received from the Canadian wheat board, signed by Mr. W. Riddel, commissioner:
In the absence of Mr. Mclvor I wish to acknowledge receipt of your telegram of November 27 last, regarding distribution of cars to the elevators at Springwater. I note that the pool elevator is receiving one third of the cars whereas the Federal Grain with two elevators but one agent is receiving two thirds of the cars being supplied.
While our board has no control over the distribution of cars at local points,-
That is a significant point.
-I wish to advise that I have brought your complaint to the attention of the railway company. 1 trust that as a result they will take some action to correct the situation.
I think here we have two very significant statements made by two significant authorities. Canadian National Railways, on the one hand, is saying that it is the responsibility of the wheat board to distribute box cars among the elevators at a marketing point. On the other hand the wheat board comes back and says it has no control over the distribution of cars, that the railway has that job. It looks to me like the old army game of trying to find the pea under the
r.Mr. Johnson (Kindersley).]
shells, but in this case the C.N.R. and the board of grain commissioners do not themselves know which shell the pea is under. It makes it very difficult for the farmers to try to figure it out. It points to the fact that legislation is necessary in the form of an amendment to the Canada Grain Act to provide a system whereby the railways and the Canadian wheat board can allocate box cars according to the wishes of the farmers among the elevators at a particular marketing point.
I believe if the principle of allowing farmers to select the elevator of their choice were introduced it would not involve too much rigidity and would not substantiate what those who oppose this bill believe, that the farmers are continuously changing from one elevator to another. I think if you take the pattern of several years' delivery at a particular point you will find that the same farmers deliver to the same elevator year after year. Conditions became particularly aggravated in periods of congestion when the elevators did not have room to accept the grain offered, and therefore the farmers had to change their pattern of delivery. Rather than being able to deliver it to the elevator to which they would prefer to deliver, they have been forced to deliver to the elevator that has space or suffer the consequences.
When you have a condition in which elevator agents and elevator companies have complete control over the purchase of grain you run across some situations which are not conducive to good farming practices. For example, the elevator agent who has a certain amount of room in his elevator is certain that it will be filled very shortly because of the necessity of the farmers to deliver grain. Therefore he does not have to concern himself with providing service to the farmer in order to induce him to deliver his grain to that elevator.
We have instances of grain elevators closing their doors sharp at six o'clock. I do not object to that, but I do object to their closing the doors at six o'clock sharp when there is a load of grain coming up the runway, and I can cite more than one instance where that has happened. The agent has become very independent. It is not his responsibility to be at the elevator. He can take up other occupations. It may be selling insurance, it may be helping one of the neighbouring farmers to combine or complete his harvesting operations. In any case he is absent from his place of business, and when a farmer comes to have a moisture test made to learn whether it is safe to harvest his grain, or to get a dockage test made or have his grain

graded so he will have some guidance as to what bin he should put it in, the agent is absent.
I think the responsibility for providing service to the farmers rests on the elevator company, and this situation has arisen through lack of competition. We have an outstanding example of that reported by Mr. M. M. MacKinnon, assistant commissioner of the board of grain commissioners. He made an investigation into the marketing situation at Tramping Lake and this is what he had to say:
Mr. P. Wisbeck, the Searle agent, advised that he is farming 300 acres. . . . The United Grain Growers' agent is also farming and has not sold any of his grain yet.
When you have a situation where companies are allowing their agents to completely disregard the service they should provide for the farmers, and are permitting them to go and farm themselves with no serious loss in their deliveries, surely you are creating a problem that needs correction. The way to do that is to amend the Canada Grain Act as set out in Bill No. 3, in order to provide farmers with an opportunity to deliver their grain to an elevator of their choice. These points I have raised would automatically be eliminated. The agent would be there providing service. He would be looking for business and wanting the farmer to deliver his grain to his elevator.
I maintain that the same principle holds with respect to agriculture that applies to other industries. I do not believe the railway rations automobile cars among the Chrysler corporation, Ford and General Motors, or that it is laid down how many cars they may get to ship their automobiles to western Canada. Cars are not given to these companies on the basis of one each. They are given to them on the basis of need, and I maintain that the same principle should hold true in the case of farmers, who should be given box cars on the basis of need. If a particular farmer wants to deliver his grain to the Federal elevator, for example, he will have the opportunity of doing so. If he wants to deliver it to the pool elevator he will have the opportunity of doing so.
That is exactly what the bill stipulates. It provides a mechanism which, as I have already mentioned, may not be perfect so far as legal terminology is concerned, because after all we are not lawyers, but I suggest that if the government really want to do something to improve this situation they could devise a workable and practical amendment among the lawyers who sit idly on the back benches.
Canada Grain Act
I would also suggest that when the time comes to vote on the bill hon. members from the wheat-growing areas should consider the people they represent and vote according to their wishes rather than according to the conscience of the Liberal party. In that way we would find all members from the wheatgrowing areas voting in support of a bill that involves the principle of allocating box cars according to the wishes of the farmers. No one can tell me that the farmers do not wish this procedure. I have had enough experience with farmers and farm meetings, and through being a practical farmer myself, to realize that this principle is most important and necessary, particularly in periods of congestion.
I am not criticizing the period of congestion. I realize the circumstances that have led up to it. We have had three excellent crops, and I would certainly commend the government and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) for at long last giving us the Canadian wheat board to market our grain and afford us some stability. The principle of marketing grain through the Canadian wheat board is one that has proved of immeasurable value to the farmers of western Canada, and I think we can improve on the system of delivering our grain by giving farmers the privilege of allocating grain to the elevators of their choice.
Finally, I say this bill covers the principles desired by the farmers, and it could be made workable. It is requested in principle by the three western pools, and it is a measure that will solve the temporary problem confronting us.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
I wish to speak in support of this amendment to the Canada Grain Act because I think it is aimed at removing an injustice which has lasted far too long. The hon. member for Assiniboia who introduced this bill, and who introduced a similar bill last year, is motivated by the hope that this injustice against the Saskatchewan pool organization can be remedied. I hope this afternoon to prove, first of all, that there is an injustice and, second, that in spite of what has been said in this house the farmers in the pool organizations do wish this injustice removed.
In the annual report of the Saskatchewan wheat pool for 1953 they set out as item No. 5 in their future policy the following:
A workable plan for the equitable distribution of cars between elevators and shipping points throughout the three provinces, on the basis of the amount of grain handled or to be handled during the season, to the end that growers may be able to deliver grain to the country elevator of their choice; at the same time preserving to the individual grower his right to order cars under the car order book sections of the Canada Grain Act.

Canada Grain Act
In that same report we find that during the crop year 1952-53 the Saskatchewan wheat pool delivered some 46 per cent of the grain. Further figures show that farmers belonging to the Saskatchewan wheat pool, who are active members of that organization, number almost 80,000 out of an estimated 112,000 farmers in that province. This means that approximately 70 per cent of the farmers in that province are members of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. It is natural to expect that these farmers, since they recover a dividend of approximately 3 cents per bushel from their own organization for the handling of that grain, would, if permitted, deliver their grain to their own organization. They would not then be assisting in the making of profits for other organizations, line companies, which have in the past exploited the farmers to the full.
Actually the number of elevators in the province is not the proper criterion by which to measure the deliveries that any pool organization would likely get. This bill is an appeal on behalf of the organizations and the farmers themselves to permit the farmers to deliver their grain to their own elevator, and thus share in the profits accruing from the handling of that grain through their own organization.
Under the present set-up the injustice results from the inequitable distribution of cars because of the failure to give instructions to train crews to see that cars are delivered to the various points according to the wishes of the farmers. Thus, instead of the pool farmers being allowed to deliver their 70 per cent of the grain, they have only been allowed to deliver 46 per cent of all grain, a loss of approximately 24 per cent. I believe the total deliveries to the farmers' organizations in 1952-53 amounted to some 214 million bushels. You can see that the failure to deliver the other 24 per cent caused the farmers a severe loss.
If you take a year when the elevators are empty and there is an opportunity for the farmers to deliver to the elevator of their choice, you will find that they will deliver 70 or 75 per cent of their grain to the wheat pool elevators. As soon as the elevators become filled, then the wheat pool deliveries drop off. The farmer must get money somewhere, and he is compelled to deliver his grain to the opposition elevators. When there are empty elevators at other points, he has to go there, or else forgo the cash advances on his grain.
It is understood that the adoption of this measure will mean more administrative work. It will require that the train crews be instructed definitely. It will require that the

wheat pool elevators at various points show what their business is. Elevators will be filled, and cars will be distributed to them in proportion to the business they are doing. It is because of the injustice in the situation that the proposal is being made. Surely a person who produces a commodity, and has an organization through which he can distribute it, should be allowed to distribute it through that organization. He should not be compelled, because of a lack of administration, to deliver the commodity to his opposition.
Perhaps members of the house would appreciate the problem if I were to make a comparison with a manufacturing concern. We will say a company manufactures refrigerators, shoes, shirts or something else, and to get that commodity to the retail market the company handles it through jobbers. What would happen if the company had its own jobbers and was suddenly, through the manipulation of box cars, delivery systems or something else, compelled to deliver that commodity to an opposition firm or through some other jobber who would not give it returns on its commodity?
The wheat pool organizations are behind this. The wheat pool members are behind this. There is a basic human right here which I feel should be recognized. The pool organizations realize that we have had a large wheat surplus for a couple of years. There is a large carryover. We might even have larger carryovers in the future, but surely if this can be done we see no reason why it should not be done. If cars can be distributed according to the wishes of the farmer so he can choose the elevator to which he wishes to deliver his grain, surely that right should not be denied to him. If the present system is continued the farmer's position might be reduced still further, and he does not look forward with any joy to helping build up his competitors. In addition to that there is the aspect of personal gain, the 3 cents per bushel. Over the past years that amount has been paid, and in some cases even more. Why should we deny that right to these farmers if there is any way of granting it?
While I was home at Christmas I made an examination of this problem. I obtained reports from the various pool committees showing the actual record of car deliveries. The car order book is operating at some points, but oddly enough we find that the train crews have avoided, if possible, spotting cars at those points where there is a car order book. In proportion, more cars were delivered to places where there was no car order book. Then the cars could be spotted in

front of the opposition elevator companies; at least that is the way it worked out. At another point where there was only one elevator, a wheat pool elevator, for some reason or other there had not been sufficient cars spotted to enable the farmers to deliver their 3 bushel quota, much less than the 5 bushel per acre quota which prevails today.
When the 5 bushel quota was announced the instructions were very definite. No cars were to be distributed to those points at which there was space in the elevators. This action meant that if the farmers wished to deliver their grain, they must deliver it to the opposition elevator companies, their own elevator being full.
There is something basically wrong here; there is a right which we think under our Canadian system should belong to every individual, namely the right of freedom of choice, to deliver his commodity to an elevator of his own choosing, particularly if it is his own. That is being denied to him. It is because of that injustice that we are bringing in this amendment, in the hope that something can be done to rectify it. There may be imperfections in it, but the basic principle and the causes behind it are sound. It is a case of justice, a case of a right that is not being given to these people. I can tell you in all sincerity that they look upon the present situation as a move on the part of some people who would like to see the Saskatchewan wheat pool and the co-operative pools of the west damaged in whatever way may be possible.
These people have carried on a fight on the western prairies for over 40 years. Throughout my lifetime I have watched the wheat pools and the co-operative organizations bit by bit getting themselves out of the clutches of the line elevator companies and the grain exchange people who operated the grain exchange to suit their own ends. When the farmers had no organization of their own and no elevators of their own they were compelled to drive up to the line elevator companies and take whatever price was offered and pay whatever price was charged for the service given. In the operation of the grain exchange the elevator companies set the price at which the wheat was sold and pocketed the millions that they obtained for the wheat.
Today, after 40 years of struggle, the farmers have their own organization; they have their own elevators. They have something over 1,100 in my own province, and they have annexes and other storage facilities there equal in number, if not greater. When they finally got their own terminals
Canada Grain Act
and their own flour mills set up they thought they would be allowed to deliver the grain to their own elevator companies. Now they have finally reached that goal they find that somebody else has put in a roadblock which prevents them from reaching the point they have been trying to get to. They are being penalized to the extent of 3 cents a bushel on about 24 per cent of the grain which is being delivered, about one-third of the wheat pool grain, and which should be going through their own elevators.
I am not able to say whether or not this bill will go through. I only know the cause is just; I only know that what they are asking for is fair. I know the organizations themselves are after it. I have not heard any real reason as to why this right should be denied them and why this principle should not be established.
Naturally, in a time of congestion such as we have at the present time some leeway must be given. It is impossible to handle all the grain through perhaps one particular elevator, but if you give these people the right to choose where they wish to go, they will be satisfied. Nobody says everything should be handled by the pool. That would be a monopoly and we do not believe in that. The farmers should be given free choice in the matter.
The facts prove that 70 per cent of the farmers in Saskatchewan are members of the wheat pool, but the facts are that so far as this 70 per cent are concerned they have a right to ask that they be given the privilege of delivering their grain to their own elevators or the elevators which they choose. In support of that we shall continue our fight.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the very fine presentations that have been made by the two hon. members who have preceded me there is little, if anything, new that I might add to this debate. However, I should like to emphasize once again some of the points which they made. At the outset I should like to make one or two observations on this problem of box car shortages.
In the last 25 years technical advances in the agricultural industry have been phenomenal. The mechanization has taken place in almost every phase of the agricultural industry, with the result that like other industries it has become a streamlined and efficient business in this country.
What we find today is a situation like this. While one end of the industry has been completely changed through technical advances and mechanization, the other end of the

Canada Grain Act
industry, namely the transportation of the products produced, is just about the same as it was 25 or 30 years ago when farmers took their grain to the market with a horse and wagon. This is one phase of the problem to which we should give some thought.
We hear a great deal about pipe lines for oil and gas. Possibly we should be giving some thought to a pipe line for wheat as a solution to this real problem of box car shortages. The problem we have to try and solve is that of the shortage of box cars. We must try to get the best, the fairest and the most equitable distribution of the facilities at hand.
In spite of everything that has been said about this bill I believe it remains a fair measure. We believe that its adoption will give the farmers of this country an equitable distribution of box cars.
The bill is in line with views held by farm organizations. As has been pointed out here this afternoon, it has been endorsed by the annual meetings of both the Saskatchewan wheat pool and the Saskatchewan farmers' union. I said there was argument against it. One of the arguments was put forward by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He said that it was physically impossible for 90 per cent of the grain to be handled through one elevator system. To some extent I doubt the validity of that argument, because I know of a great many places in the province where there is only one elevator, and it does not seem to have too much trouble taking all the wheat in that area that is designated to be put through that elevator.
Another argument put forward is that it will interfere with the car order book. I have heard that several times and of course it is absolutely untrue, because the bill as presented is very explicit in that regard. It is intended to apply only where the car order book is not in effect.
While I am speaking about the car order book, I should like to say something more about it. I think we have to support the provisions respecting the car order book in the Canada Grain Act until we have something that is going to work better. I am of the opinion that the provisions regarding the car order book are completely antiquated, for the simple reason that the original purpose of the car order book in the main does not apply at this time. I am sure one of the main reasons the car order book was instituted in the first place was to protect the farmers in western Canada from the unfair practices they had to contend with in the private grain trade as to grades and weight, which of course reflected ultimately in the price they received for their product.

Those unfair practices do not apply at the present time in so far as the private grain trade is concerned. I am of the opinion that the private grain trade will give as good service as the pools, but I hasten to add that they are giving that service because of the presence of pool elevators throughout the country which constitute a threat to their very existence unless they deal fairly with the producer. That is one reason I believe the car order book is more or less obsolete at the present time.
One other reason why I believe it is inadequate is that set forth by the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he referred to the suspension of the car order book. He said, as reported on page 939 of Hansard of December 15, 1953:
With the absolute need for priority shipments, the distribution of cars in accordance with the applications in the car order book cannot be properly carried out. To check every application to ensure that the grain to be shipped has a preference is impossible, and would unnecessarily delay shipments.
Looking at it from that point of view I think it is pretty safe to say that the car order book is not as important as it might be.
As I said a moment ago, I doubt if anything I can say will add to the fine presentation we have heard already. The arguments by the minister with regard to the suspension of the car order book do not seem to be very valid. It must be remembered that at the time of its suspension it applied only to 200 points out of some 1,200 in Saskatchewan, and did not apply in either Alberta or Manitoba.
In conclusion may I point out again that I believe the proposals outlined in the bill now before us are fair and have the support of farm organizations and farm people in western Canada. I am sure their adoption will make for a more equitable distribution of box cars.

Mr. Speaker, I believe there has been a very good discussion of this bill, and from that discussion I think it is clear that if it becomes law it will provide a fair, equitable and workable method of distributing box cars.
When the Minister of Trade and Commerce enters a debate he usually takes a very decided position. He opposed this bill, but in doing so I think he made one of his milder presentations. The minister claimed that this bill would make the distribution of

box cars more rigid. Then in the very next sentence he complained that the bill was not rigid enough. He said that another difficulty in the bill was that it did not require the farmer to deliver grain to a particular elevator. First the minister said it was too rigid and then he said it was not rigid enough. The minister went on to say, and I quote from page 935 of Hansard of December 15, 1953:
We are not discussing grain marketing in general but a particular bill related to it, and if there are weaknesses in that bill, obviously the bill should be opposed whether you like the principle or not.
I submit that that is no reason for defeating this bill. Rather the subject matter of the bill should be referred to the agriculture committee of this house for discussion and consideration. The problem of the distribution of box cars in western Canada is serious. Its solution is urgent, and I believe members of parliament should be giving consideration to a solution of that problem.
I think most hon. members in the house agree that the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce is particularly able. I have enough confidence in the minister to believe that he could bring forth a workable solution to this problem if he cared to. There is just one difficulty. If a workable solution to the distribution of box cars is brought forward it will allow farmers to deliver grain to the elevator of their choice. When they are able to do that it will mean more grain for their own elevator system and less grain for the private elevator system.
The minister said he had never heard any complaints from the wheat pool organization about the distribution of box cars. Well, I certainly have. They complained in their latest annual report. A committee of the three western wheat pools have been considering this problem for the last year. A resolution was passed at their most recent convention asking for a proper and fair distribution of box cars.
I hope when the vote is taken members from all sides of the house will support the bill. I was glad to note that we are receiving support from members of the Social Credit party. I am hopeful that we will receive some support from western members of the Conservative party. The problem is certainly urgent; it must be solved, and to say that it does not exist is not being realistic.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Cote -Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair:
That it is expedient to amend the Post Office Act to increase the rates of postage on letters posted in Canada from the 1st day of April, 1954,
(a)	on each letter for delivery within the postal area in which it is posted, from three cents to four cents for the first ounce or fraction of an ounce, and from one cent to two cents for each additional ounce or fraction of an ounce, and
(b)	on each letter posted within one postal area for delivery in another postal area from four cents to five cents for the first ounce or fraction of an ounce, and from two cents to three cents for each additional ounce or fraction of an ounce.
