speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while a good many members on this side of the house have entered the debate, nevertheless I feel that people outside the house and particularly in my part of the province of New Brunswick are becoming more interested as more is said here.
One point has been brought to my attention from my own province since this debate started. I have no desire to criticize the Post Office Department and' the congenial minister in particular, inasmuch as he is one person with whom it is difficult to argue because he is very co-operative. I also believe I can honestly say that in general the post office officials give exceptionally good service and sometimes, as in the case of my own constituency, under most difficult circumstances. But I understand that the increase in postage rates is not being introduced for the purpose of increasing or improving the service. Like other speakers I say that neither I nor the people whom I represent believe that this tax-and it is a tax-this increase in postage rates is being imposed solely for the purpose of meeting increased expenditure in the department.
In other words, having in mind the farsightedness of the Minister of Finance, we do not believe it can honestly be said' that this situation could not have been anticipated when the budget was brought down last

February. We also feel that there is discrimination, and I will come back to that in a few minutes. However, as the Postmaster General said, let us be fair about this matter. Let us examine the facts as the government has placed them before us and as it placed them before the people last summer and in the budget debate last spring. When the Minister of Finance brought down his budget he reviewed very ably the financial situation of the country. After making that review he told us that he was going to eliminate the stamp tax on cheques. He could very well do so because he was still budgeting for quite a considerable surplus.
At the very time he was doing that, at the very time he was telling hon. members that he could dispense with the stamp tax on cheques, he also knew that he was going to take away a tremendous amount of revenue from the Post Office Department. I am satisfied of that, and I think any member of the house, knowing the Minister of Finance, knew very well that the minister realized that the department would suffer. For over 20 years this department has contributed millions of dollars to the consolidated revenue fund. About eight or nine months after removing the stamp tax the Post Office Department found itself in financial difficulties. Why? I am not convinced that this was a surprise to them, and' I do not think any member can say, after listening to the arguments put forward in the house in the last two days, that anyone should be surprised who knew the situation prior to last February.
Therefore the government knew quite well when they removed the stamp tax that something had to be done for the Postmaster General. The Minister of Finance budgeted for a surplus, and as far as we know he is going to achieve it. Let him turn over part of that surplus to the Post Office Department to meet its expenses for this year. Give the Postmaster General a chance to put into operation some of the recommendations made by the firm of consultants which investigated the department at their request. I understand he is starting to implement them. Give him a year to see what economies he can put into effect. Give him a year to see what the picture will be. I am very doubtful that there will be much of a deficit, because I believe the Postmaster General is just as efficient as any other minister and his department can be run just as efficiently as any other. Give him a chance to see what he can do, and if it is necessary to provide funds to meet a deficit let them be provided out of the

consolidated revenue fund, because over the years that fund has received millions of dollars from the department.
If the government do not consider that is the fair thing to do, then they will have to face the criticism which is going to be made, and which I believe we are quite justified in making, that the stamp tax on cheques was removed simply as an election promise and for no other reason. It is a tax. I do not care whether you call it postage; I say it is still a tax. It comes out of the people.
Coming back to the question of discrimination, the stamp tax on cheques was paid largely by the people who could better afford to pay it, but now everybody who happens to write a letter is going to have to pay the higher postage rate.
There is another point in connection with discrimination. From what has been said here there seems to be no doubt that the air mail rate is going to be reduced. It is going to be eliminated, if you wish, because all mail will carry a 5-cent postage stamp for the first ounce. I happen to live in an area where very few people use the air mail service. If I want to send a message from my home to Ottawa it will arrive here quicker by train than by plane. That is the case for all of the area I represent, because we are so far from an airport that by the time a letter has been mailed in the post office and taken to the airport it will take longer to reach Ottawa than if sent by train. But we will have to pay the same amount of postage on our mail as will those people who can and do use air mail service substantially.
As one of my colleagues said this afternoon, if a person wants to use the air mail service he can do so. I do not think anybody has been kicking about paying the extra postage, but let those people pay for the service who want it and use it. We do not want air mail service because in our community it is of no particular benefit to us. It does not seeem to do us much good. If we happened to be sending letters to Vancouver, Victoria or other places in the west we might get some advantage from it, but most of our people do business with people in Montreal, Toronto, Ottawa and other points in the east. If they want to use air mail they are quite willing to pay for it, and that is the opinion I have received today from my constituency.
Last night the hon. member for Charlotte said that as far as he knew nobody in New Brunswick was kicking. That may have been true up to the point when people began to wake up to the fact that this was simply a case of robbing Peter to pay Paul, that it was a case of removing a tax in one place
Post Office. Act
and imposing it in another. There is, therefore, some opposition to this increase in the postage rate.

In the annual report of the Postmaster General for last year we find a sentence to the effect that the department has received assistance from the firm of J. D. Woods, Limited, management consultants. This was the report to which I referred yesterday in this house, saying that we had not seen it. The minister was kind enough to say that he would make it available to me for whatever use I wanted to make of it.
I want to thank him for doing so. I am sorry he could not lend me a copy of the report, because I did find it a little difficult working on the corner of his secretary's desk throughout this morning and studying the report while she dictated to a succession of three of her secretaries. Apparently there is no shortage of staff in the hierarchy of the Post Office Department. Perhaps that is the reason it just seemed to the minister yesterday that he had 50,000 people instead of the
44,000	he actually has.
Before we examine the statements made in this report, I think two general points should be made. First of all the report was commissioned by the department itself, which

Post Office Act
paid many thousands of dollars for it. I do not know how much. Perhaps the minister might tell us. From having seen other jobs of this kind done, I would imagine it cost between $10,000 and $15,000 for the complete job. It is quite obvious, therefore, that the department is to a certain extent, as in all these cases, in a position to suggest to the group doing the job the nature of the treatment that should be undertaken, and perhaps in a certain way how their remarks might be phrased.
I think this is particularly important, because as I understand it the government has a number of jobs of this kind which are done from time to time, and it is quite obvious that any firm would want to retain this connection. When the report is critical, it is no defence to say you will take measures to correct this situation unless the criticism contained in this report is very limited. Throughout the whole of this report we find generalized criticism of the department which indicates a state of affairs that can only be solved by a general housecleaning. There has been no indication in the department's annual report or in anything that has been said in this house that there is going to be any general housecleaning of the Post Office Department.
We must remember also that in its own report for this year the Post Office Department has said that it has for a number of years been devoting a great deal of time and effort to management and organizational problems.
If the department has been doing that for a great many years, and a report is written concerning their operations at the end of 1952, we would logically expect to find the department in fairly good shape. On the other hand, if after all this an independent organization paid by the government to study a government operation is still critical of that operation, then surely we are correct in assuming there is something wrong with that department. The department has demonstrated its inability to correct the situation.
We come now to the report itself. It opens with a glowing sentence praising the Post Office Department. As I have already said, that is what we would logically expect to find. After all, the government paid for it. The opening sentence says that the firm has been impressed by the over-all efficiency of the department, the basic soundness of its administration and organization. That is almost standard in any reports where companies are involved, as any of you who have seen these reports know. As we have said, the government is paying for it. This is very

much the same sort of thing as the Dale Carnegie principle which says that you say something nice before you criticize. It is along the lines of the standard sales technique which is to the effect that everything you say is fine, but-and then you give the fellow the truth.
We must not be misled, therefore, by a few statements-and there are a few-in the report which commend the department. I leave those for the minister to bring up later. The basic fact is the report recommends a complete and sweeping reorganization of this department, implying that it is poorly organized, poorly run, inefficient in many cases, and that savings of hundreds of thousands a year could be made in one operation in one city.
It is said that previous recommendations by the civil service commission for increased efficiency have not been followed; that physical facilities presently available for the receipt, storage and dispatch of postage stamps and unemployment insurance stamps are inadequate, both from the viewpoint of security and material handling. Later on I am going to bolster all this with specific quotations from the report.
The report makes over 75 major recommendations of one kind or another. To my mind that is a clear indication of the sorry state of the department now. The recommendations in that report, and I am not going to list them here, range from radical reorganization of lines of authority, decentralization of much activity, and complete changes in the personnel operation, to the establishment of new divisions, increases in the special delivery rates and improvement in the service and reorganization of the tender procedure. The report continues by suggesting such things as the introduction of a system ensuring direct review of services provided for the public so that the complaints and requests of the public may be anticipated.
If 75 sweeping changes of this nature can be logically recommended by this organization, then something is certainly wrong within the department.

I thank you, sir, for that. These are notes. I presume I can start over again and have another 40 minutes because of these interruptions.

Now let us turn to an examination of some, not all, of the specific charges made in this report. Here is what the report says regarding planning:
It is apparent that the number of clerical staff presently available for this type of work is completely inadequate to deal with the problems being encountered throughout the department.
That idea is bolstered again in another section of the report. We shall now deal with the section having to do with the present method of operation. It says:
Many of the problems raised by the postmasters . . . are referred to the operations branch at headquarters for decision. This system requires the staff at headquarters to deal with a multitude of individual problems . . . The staff at headquarters operate under continuous pressure and there are many delays in dealing with comparatively minor matters. The staff are so occupied in this routine that they are unable to develop and apply policy decisions which would eliminate many individual requests.
If I may say so, it is necessary that I put this on the record because the report is not available to us. I have had the opportunity of studying it, and this is the only way I can put it on the record so the people of Canada can see what is happening in the Post Office Department. In giving these quotations I am abbreviating somewhat but retaining the nature of the quotation and the words used in the report.
With regard to the operations branch the report says:
The work of the operations branch has over the years increased to the point where the staff at all levels are overloaded with a multitude of routine problems and correspondence. No one has had the time to develop policies which can be applied on an over-all basis.
Is it any wonder, when we see these things unfolding before us, that the Post Office Department finds it necessary to come and ask for an increase in the postage rates? Is it any wonder they should do that with this type of internal organization?
Turning to the buildings which are used by the post office we find the report saying:
It is essential that detailed consideration be given to new construction in order that the most efficient operating methods be incorporated in the design.
Quite properly, the postal superintendent in charge of the buildings division has concentrated on this phase of his activities. All the staff in the division have been so engaged. They have not had time to seek out and introduce operating economies throughout the existing post offices. Our survey has disclosed that there is room for substantial savings through better layout, equipment and control.
The post office needs information; it needs controls. Here is one of the things the report has to say regarding controls:
The branch is operating under a severe handicap as there are no standards established to measure the relative efficiency of a given method of operation. The lack of such standards is particularly
Post Office Act
felt when requests are received for additions to staff or accommodation. The only relative comparison of the volume of work in various post offices is the revenue received by each for the services it renders to the public. It is recognized by the department that this is not an adequate yardstick due to the varying conditions under which post offices operate. The lack of such a standard also makes it difficult to appraise the benefits which might be obtained from improvements in methods and equipment.
We have here another indication why the department is operating largely in the dark, yet it comes to us asking for an increase in rates. We know now, on the basis of the information which is going on the record, that really this department knows not whereof it speaks.
Another section of the report deals with the mechanical engineering division, which is a new department suggested by this report, and I quote:
A mechanical engineering division should make a detailed examination of the equipment and layout presently in use in post offices. This study will disclose great differences in the equipment. In some instances, equipment installed many years ago was continued in use although more efficient equipment is now available. No attempt has been made to standardize on the most efficient equipment.
The report goes on:
There is a need for a reappraisal of the services being provided at various centres across the country. The department should be continually examining the nature of services provided and prepared to make alterations as required to keep pace with changing conditions.
There is very clearly a suggestion there that the department is not doing that; that it is static; that it is not keeping abreast of what is going on in the world.
We now come to another section of the report, regarding a methods and procedures division. The report says:
This division would be responsible for preparing and amending operating manuals. This is presently the responsibility of the services, methods and examinations division. The staff available for this work has proved inadequate and the existing manuals were, in many cases, issued years ago and are now in a large extent obsolete.
The production of up-to-date operating manuals should more than repay the expenditure involved in staff salaries required to prepare them. At the present time there are numerous errors occurring throughout the service and the correction of each one requires the expenditure of time and labour.
We now come to the question of workshops which the department is operating. I never knew that the post office operated workshops. This is what the report says:
At headquarters in Ottawa and a number of the large centres across the country workshops under the supervision of local plant engineers have been established . . .
Then comes an interesting point, because we find that these workshops have been

Post Office Act
greatly enlarged so that they are doing something else. Here is the quotation from the report:
It was noted during our survey that a number of these workshops have extended their activities to the manufacture of equipment such as cupboards, wastepaper containers, binneys, and skids, and to the repair of typewriters and other office equipment.
The Post Office Department is in the office equipment business. The report goes on:
These workshops were not established for this purpose and it is questionable if this type of work is economical.
It is suggested that a detailed study of the actual staff requirements to carry out the essential repair work be made and the staff be reduced to a minimum required to perform these duties.
I should now like to give hon. members an item in the report which vjjll capture the imagination of Canadians across this country more than anything else in it. After all, what I have shown so far is fundamental; terribly important, but it is fundamental; it is the organization and operation of the department. Here are three ideas for this committee which show clearly where the department is not taking advantage of current operating methods and the information available to it in order to save the taxpayers' money. Item 1 has to do with floor space and reads as follows:
Floor space,-a redesign of a letter-sorting rack in the forward letter section of the Toronto post office, and improved layout of these racks would result in a 45 per cent saving in the floor space used for this purpose. The changes would not have any significant effect on the labour cost of the operation as it is presently performed.
Item 2 is as follows:
Equipment design. The use of conveyor belts and changes in equipment would allow two operations to be combined.
I understand that this refers to Toronto. Hon. members understand that I have not the report immediately in front of me. The minister has it. There are minor matters which I have no doubt he will correct me on, but there are no major ones.
I am giving just a few of the quotations from the report, which goes on to say that a change in the equipment used would allow these operations to be combined.
While this plan will require further development there is an indicated annual saving in the forward letter section of the Toronto post office alone of approximately $200,000 per annum.
This is referring only to Toronto, and it states it will require further development; but there is indicated an annual saving in the forward letter section of the Toronto post office alone of approximately $200,000 per annum. Let us make it quite clear that this $200,000 saving is possible after the

necessary equipment and everything else connected with the operation is installed. That would mean the taxpayers of this country would have to pay to the Post Office Department $200,000 a year less. Putting it another way, the expenses of the Post Office Department would be $200,000 a year less.
With regard to the work place lay-out, the report states that a rearrangement of the lay-out equipment used for sorting tables would increase the efficiency of the operation by from 10 to 26 per cent, with resulting reductions in staff.
Let those three examples be impressed in the minds of everyone as an indication of what is happening today in the Post Office Department, and the tremendous savings of hundreds upon hundreds of thousands of dollars that it would be possible to make if this department would smarten up and operate in the most efficient and economical way.
The report then goes on to refer to the special delivery service. It is interesting to note that for reasons best known to himself the minister decided this year to raise the other rates of postage but not the special delivery rates. The report states:
The cost Information available to the department discloses that the special delivery service is operated at a considerable loss. In some centres the postal rate for a special delivery letter is less than the contractor is paid to deliver the letter. The user of the special delivery service is interested in a rapid and assured delivery. It is believed that the majority of users would be prepared to pay considerably more for this service if their requirements were met.
The special delivery is used by only a small number of people, but it is not paying its way; yet in the case of another service the rates are increased. At this point I should like to make just a passing reference to another item in the report which I think is tremendously significant. I am surprised that neither the government nor the Postmaster General has seen fit to make some mention of this matter at some point. There is a suggestion in the report that the post office savings bank, once a most vital part of the economy of this country, has now largely outlived its usefulness, that there is little demand for it. The report recommends categorically that this operation of the Post Office Department be abolished, and it points out that a saving of $377,000 could be made in that one particular instance.
I am not committing myself, nor do I intend to get into a debate on the question of the abolition of the post office savings bank, but here is a potential saving of

$377,000 mentioned in this report of which we knew nothing. No one outside the confines of the minister's office, as far as I can find out, knew of this until last night when for reasons which I should like to think were good the minister made the report available to me.
With regard to the transportation and carriage of mail the report says:
Little effort has been made to appraise the whole transportation problem and to develop a rational plan or policy to govern future operations and methods.
The report continues with a discussion of subsidies as an important factor in the operation of the Post Office Department. It states:
The need for a subsidy should, however, become less as an area grows and the volume of normal traffic increases. In the past in negotiating contracts no effort has been made to set out the amount that has been paid as subsidy as opposed to what might be described as the normal cost of operation.
And again:
The subsidy may therefore be perpetuated long after the justification for it has ceased to exist.
Then with regard to the railway mail service division the report states:
At the present time there is no one senior officer at headquarters responsible for the over-all direction of the railway mail service.
There is much more in the report. Then another quotation:
A limited survey of the conditions in Toronto discloses that the planning of this pick-up and delivery service has not been given the consideration which it deserves.
I come now to a reference to how they handle their stamps, which represent money. The report states:
The postage supply section of the postage stamp division is responsible primarily for the receipt, storage and dispatch of postage and unemployment insurance stamps to postal depots and government agencies. The physical facilities presently available for this purpose are inadequate both from the viewpoint of security and material handling. Many improvements in procedure could also be made.
Then follows an important matter which I believe others of my colleagues will take up and comment on later. The report goes on to say:
We have reviewed a report of the civil service commission. A comprehensive analysis was made in 1950 of the method of keeping records and issuing stock. It is suggested that this report be reviewed and the suggestions put into practice.

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of bringing to the attention of the Postmaster General any personal complaints with regard to the delivery of mail. Over the years I have received from the post office nothing but excellent service. Consequently I have no letters to produce that have been delayed in delivery. I have none to produce that have been incorrectly addressed or anything of that nature. In fact, what disturbs me so frequently with regard to the postal delivery is that some letters I would prefer not to receive arrive with great promptness. I would be perfectly happy if they were delayed for several weeks. I have never been quite able to understand why a letter advising me that I have overlooked some account or other arrives the day after it is mailed.
I should like to pay my respects to the postal employees who, over the years, have delivered mail at my home. They have been looking after me extremely well during the last few years. I find that their work is very well done and I am perfectly satisfied. I have no complaints on those scores at all.
I intend to direct any suggestions I may have to make with regard to the administration in general and to the Postmaster General himself. I think one of the reasons this debate has gone on as long as it has at the resolution stage is the fact that the Postmaster General took an improper approach to this problem. It is a matter of experience, I suppose. We all learn. If, on the introduction of the resolution yesterday, the Postmaster General had given a detailed explanation of the operation of the postal department and had given the figures and the statistics to prove conclusively that an increase in postal rates was needed, I think perhaps this debate would have been over long before this time. It is because. ,hat information has not been given to us that we have been searching for it from this side of the house.
For example, on a first reading of what the minister said yesterday one would be inclined to think there will be increased costs

for postal service next year, that we must therefore have increased revenue to look after that opportunity. He should have said, as that Nothing at all is said with regard to any of the economies that might be introduced, and nothing at all with regard to the nature of the postal service and its effect on and importance to our country.
The Postmaster General had an opportunity of presenting a broad picture of the importance of postal service in Canada. He missed that opportunity. He should have said, as that great postmaster general who has been mentioned earlier, Sir William Mulock, said, something about the nature of the postal service and its importance. These are words of Sir William Mulock which were quoted yesterday:
Public opinion favours the cheapest and freest possible communication by mail throughout all parts of the country.
I think that holds true today just as surely as it did in the days when Sir William Mulock made the statement. I think the present Postmaster General should have emphasized that point and pointed out to us the nature of the postal service in Canada. He should have disclosed to us what in his opinion is the business part and what is the public service part, because these things should be clearly understood. If you are going to consider the postal service merely as a business, then you balance expenditures against revenues and you say that this or that must be done. But there are other factors concerned.
Again this afternoon I thought the Postmaster General's replies to the statements made yesterday by hon. members were inadequate. I think I recall him saying yesterday that so many things were discussed during the course of the day that he could not begin to answer them all at that time. He had an opportunity today, and we would have been quite content to listen to him for a considerable period if he had dealt point by point with the matters raised by hon. members on this side of the house. But he summarized very rapidly. He said-and I hope I am quoting him correctly or at least giving the gist of his remarks-that those who have spoken in this debate so far can be divided into those who think the users of the postal service should pay and those who think everybody should pay. There was more to it than that.
There was certainly a third view expressed by member after member on this side of the house. Granted that there were those who said the users should pay; granted that there were those who said everybody should pay, but what about the remarks that were made 83276-75*

about the increased business that might result for the post office through greater efficiency? What about the remarks about searching for other sources of revenue? What about the remarks reviewing accounting procedures within the department, and the suggestions that some of the subsidies to other governmental departments and to Trans-Canada Air Lines, for example, might be discontinued?
Surely this was a different point of view from the two the Postmaster General mentioned, and I regret to say that the Postmaster General did not deal with these matters. Then we had set out for us yesterday by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, who has made such a splendid contribution to this debate, the surpluses and the deficits over a long period of years. I think this is the type of background material that the Postmaster General should have given us-We were informed that for the first 30 years-following confederation there was a series of unending deficits and that then, with the change in postal procedure and a reduction in postal rates, surpluses resulted in the second 30 years. There were twenty-two surpluses and nine deficits, but on balance surpluses. There was a surplus for that 30-year period.
For the last 20 years we had our attention drawn to the fact that there had been eighteen surpluses and two very small deficits, resulting in a surplus of $90 million for the final 20-year period.

I think that is not quite good enough when we are dealing with a matter as important as this.
This then is the objection I make on this occasion with respect to this important matter, and it is important because it affects everybody in the country. There are some who say that people do not write letters. I have never met anyone who did not write a letter or did not receive letters. In some way the postal service affects everybody in the country. In a matter as important as this I think we should have had full information, but we have been dependent on this side of the house to provide that information.

Post Office Act
Look at the research that has been done by the hon. member for Hamilton West, the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, the hon. member for Danforth and others on this side of the house who have done the reading, compiled statistics and presented a picture to us of the functioning of the Post Office Department over the years. Why did we not have that presented by the Postmaster General himself? I think he missed a very great opportunity there. In my opinion sufficient information has been disclosed in the course of the debate to indicate that there are a great many ways of saving on the postal service; that there are ways and means of increasing, we hope, the efficiency of the service, and that these should be explored before an increase in the first-class postal rate is put into effect.
The Postmaster General neglected to give us a picture of the future of Canada. Are we not expecting great things? Do we not hear from other ministers of the crown about our expanding economy? Do we not hear about the increase in our population and the general advance of Canada? Is it not right to expect that as our population increases postal service will increase, and that additional revenue will be produced from that source?
The statistics shown in the minister's annual report, and the ones upon which I think he based his expected revenue from the addition of one cent on first-class mail, show that per capita about 100 pieces of first class mail are carried by the post office during the year, and the corresponding revenue from that source. Our population, by natural increase and by immigration, is increasing yearly at a rate-I will use round figures-of about 300,000. On a per capita basis that should surely indicate almost a million dollars additional revenue to the Post Office Department with each succeeding year.
The Postmaster General has not taken that into account in his consideration of this problem. Had a proper picture been presented to us it would have made it much simpler for us to consider the whole problem. We might have been saved some of this lengthy discussion, and perhaps we would have been less critical of the Postmaster General and the administration of his department. We would like an assurance from him that the Post Office Department is going to continue to serve the people of Canada with greater efficiency, with speedier service; that the revenue of the Post Office Department will increase on that account; that there will be a reorganization so the department is bearing only those expenditures that are properly

those of the Post Office Department, and so on. Such information, however, was not forthcoming.
I believe the Postmaster General still has an opportunity this evening to deal with some of these matters and answer some of the questions that have been raised on this side of the house. He should tell us, for the information of members and the people of Canada, the place the postal service has in this country, and' what part of it is strictly business and what part of it is a public service.

There are one or two problems I should like to mention which are peculiar to suburban ridings. I should like to comment on the regulation which prevents two sub-post offices from being within a statute mile of one another. I think that regulation is archaic, for this reason. The suburban highways leading from our metropolitan centres are six and eight lane roads. Traffic travels both ways along those roads at an average of 40 miles an hour, although 30 miles per hour is the statutory speed limit. When one has eight lanes of traffic travelling at that speed, it is as difficult and dangerous to cross that road as it is to cross the Niagara river.
The regulation states that if a sub-post office is on one side of the road another subpost office cannot be situated within a mile of it, even although it is on the other side of the road. It is obvious that these main highways and this traffic present a barrier which, while not constituting a statute mile, is at the same time a hazard and an obstacle far greater than the statutory distance. I only hope that when this matter is dealt with this regulation will be reconsidered, particularly as it affects suburban municipalities. There have been several sub-post offices, and one in particular, at which a great deal of

congestion has taken place simply because no other post office can be located closer than one mile.

Certain it is that we have many more towns and municipalities benefiting by reason of house to house delivery than we had years ago. a prominent firm of management consultants would whet the interest and certainly the curiosity of an opposition which is charged with inquiring into these very things. Yes; I can imagine the minister's chagrin that probably these facts were produced before he himself had an opportunity of giving a full report, but it is a fact that four months after this report was received, in the departmental report of March 31, 1953, there is what might be considered a mild sort of boast that considerable progress has been made with changes in organization along the lines suggested. Broadly, the recommendations provide for greater decentralization of responsibility for operations into the field organization; strengthening and reorganization of staffs at headquarters so that senior officials may be able to devote more of their time and energy to over-all operational study and planning; strengthening of the engineering organization at headquarters to provide the means for time and motion studies, greater designing facilities and the setting up of standards for application throughout the service; intensification of research and planning in the field of transportation; further development of cost controls, so as to make available information on which to base decisions affecting all aspects of the service.
It would be a very incurious person indeed, Mr. Chairman, whose curiosity would not be whetted by this general statement of what the department was undertaking as a result of having received this report.
While I have no intention of quoting the report clause by clause, I might say that every hon. member should be interested in knowing just what savings can be effected by the implementation of the report brought down by a very capable firm of management engineers after months of study. It would be interesting to know also what has been discovered in the field of tenders, because the minister will remember that on a number of occasions we have discussed tenders in the house.
No doubt under this heading the suggestion would cover a very broad field. We would be interested to know that; we would be interested also to know what has been discovered with reference to the operations

of the post office savings bank. It is true that in some centres of this country it is the only bank that is available to the people in that locality, but in a great many other places it is simply an additional service provided in a centre where other banks are and have been operating, and generally speaking take care of the requirements of the citizens of the locality.
I see that in the current report-if I have overlooked it I apologize-no mention is made of the loss in that department for this year, although in 1946 the loss on the operation of the post office savings bank was given as over $260,000. If that was the loss in 1946 I would think you could reasonably expect that it would be half as much again today, and that is a sizeable amount of money. You are getting well up toward half a million dollars.
I should like to quote one or two other very interesting suggestions which were made, and on which we may be pardoned for having reasonable curiosity. We can take the remark which appears on page 33 of the report and which reads:
The work of the operations branch has over the years increased to the point where the staff at all levels are overloaded with a multitude of routine problems and correspondence.
Then there is another matter which to my mind is most important to a department handling the volume of not only mail but also parcels, all of which pass through the post office. I refer to materials handling. I suppose the whole field of materials handling has received more expert study in the last ten years in industry generally than almost any other phase, with the possible exception of accounting by tabulating machines. If, as is indicated in this report, the materials handling in the Post Office Department is many years behind the times, then we would be interested to learn in what way the department proposes to remedy that situation, and what they estimate the savings to the department will be by reason of accepting these recommendations.
As I said a moment ago, Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to go into the Woods and Gordon report. That does not mean I am not curious about it. On the contrary, I shall watch with great interest for some report from the Post Office Department as to just what has taken place. But I do say that the Postmaster General has probably been given a most unsavoury task. Whether that is true or not, I would say that it is in my estimation a most audacious move to come before this parliament and propose an increase in the postal rates of this nation, to ask the people of Canada to give to a department

something in the nature of $15 million more revenue, when that department has not the least idea what it needs this money for. Neither has it any idea just where it can save a sizeable amount of money, and that despite the fact that they have in their hands, and have had now for some 14 months, an excellent report which might very well have been implemented before this request came to the people of this country through this parliament.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during the last few days there has been considerable discussion from the other side of the house with regard to this suggested raise in postage rates, and it has been said by hon. members on the other side that hon. members on this side have taken very little interest in this matter. The position of the government is not a happy one, and they know it; but when the government has to raise rates by one cent in order to provide services and give its employees dollars and cents and not lip service, we are ready to support the stand of the government in that regard.
During the debate some mention has been made of the 5-cent defeat of this government, but it seems to me that for the last two days the taxpayers of Canada have been paying for campaign speeches by hon. members across the floor.
Another thing that more or less amazed me was the statement by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton that he could pay 4 cents and get better service than air mail by putting his letter on the train. There are other parts of Canada where we have to pay 7 cents in order to get the same service he gets for 4 cents, and we will be most happy with this 5-cent rate across the board under which we will receive the same service as the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton is getting for 4 cents. I think it is about time we got it.
Post Office Act
Resolution agreed to: Yeas, 49; nays, 34.
